Content: One-variable data, also known as univariate data, focuses on a single characteristic or metric collected across a group of individuals or items. While multi-variable data tries to find connections between different traits, one-variable data looks closely at the behavior and patterns of a single metrics - such as the test scores of a classroom, the heights of trees in an orchard, or the lifespans of a batch of lightbulbs. In the real world, analyzing one-variable data is the math that facilitates quality control, logistics, and public health.

On the SAT exam, mastering one-variable data is essential for working through the Problem Solving and Data Analysis category. Many SAT problems place an emphasis on data literacy, which measures our ability to interpret data sets in various visual formats. For example, we might see visual display of data and be tasked with calculating or estimating a statistic, comparing two different datasets, or determine the effect of an outlier. Learning to interpret the features of many types of statistical graphics lets us quickly draw statistical conclusions for a particular dataset.

The key concept that describes all one-variable data is the distribution. A distribution describes the complete profile of a dataset, showing all the possible values and exactly how often each value shows up. It reveals the underlying shape - most importantly, the center and spread of the data — whether the numbers are tightly clustered, spread out evenly, or leaning mostly toward one side with outliers on the other end.

To display distributions, the SAT exam include a variety of highly predictable tables and graphs. The most basic format is a frequency table, which is a simple two-column lists that describes all the distinct values or intervals along with the number of times (or frequency) those values appear. A histogram takes the data from a frequency table and transforms it into a bar chart, where distinct values or intervals (called bins) are on the horizontal axis and the height of each bar matches the frequency of those values.

Dot plots are another type of visual distribution that is well suited for small, clustered datasets. A dot plot lists values along a standard number line and places a stack of dots above each value to represent its frequency. This format allows you to see every single data point clearly as an individual dot, so it's an excellent tool for quickly finding exact statistics - like the middle or most frequent value.

Box plot (also known as a box-and-whisker plot) test our understanding of the spread of a distribution across in different quartiles. Unlike histograms or dot plots, a box plot does not display individual data points or their exact frequencies. Instead, it gives an overview of a distribution using a five-number summary: the minimum value, the first quartile (`Q_1`), the median value (`Q_2`), the third quartile (`Q_3`), and the maximum value. The box contains the middle `50%` of the data, stretching from `Q_1` to `Q_3`, with a vertical line splitting the box at the exact median. The “whiskers” extend outward to the minimum and maximum boundaries.

On the SAT exam, these distinct visual layouts dictate our analytical strategy and which statistics we can actually determine. Certain problems might ask to identify the median or the range as well as how an extreme outlier will shift the appearance across different types of graphics. Recognizing the specific rules of each graphic helps to quickly understand how small changes to the data will affect the distribution visually. With dot plots or frequency tables, any change in the data will create a visual change. However, because box plots display boundaries between segments of data at a summary, changing an individual value doesn't necessarily affect the visual.
